title: New Deal Texas and the West
description_text:
Inspired by the 90th anniversary of the New Deal (1933-1943), the exhibition New Deal Texas and the West features federally funded art produced by American artists during the Great Depression (1929-1941) and collected by The Dallas Museum of Art.  Focusing especially on New Deal art produced in and about Texas, the exhibition also includes images and objects of scenes and subjects in the Western states of New Mexico and Oklahoma, and work made across the nation in media ranging from murals and prints to sculptures and textiles.  This exhibition is organized by The University of Texas at Dallas in collaboration with The Dallas Museum of Art. On view at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum.

Athenaeum hours: 11 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Sunday. Free admission.

 

Image: Blanche McVeigh, Men Working on West Lancaster, c. 1933–1934, aquatint, Dallas Museum of Art, gift of the Public Works of Art Project.

title: SPARK Femmes (Sex and Pornography Addiction Recovery Kit)
description_text:
We are collecting interest to choose a time/date for this semester. If you are interested, please reach out to sccgroups@utdallas.edu with your availability, and group will begin once we have enough students and a time/day is chosen.

SPARK Femmes is a supportive, nonjudgmental space for women and femmes who are questioning or struggling with the ways they engage with sex and/or pornography. Because these concerns can carry especially intense shame, stigma, and isolation for women and femmes, the group is designed to offer a private, affirming space where students can speak openly without fear of judgment.

Participants will have opportunities to process their experiences, explore what healthy sexuality means for them, and build practical tools for navigating urges, distress, shame, relationships, and recovery. Whether this is an issue that has only recently become concerning or something you have been navigating for a long time, SPARK Femmes will meet you where you are.

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: Emotional Resilience Skills & Support Drop-In
description_text:
Powerful emotions can feel overwhelming, but learning how to work with them makes a difference. This support group is a weekly space to connect, share, and practice ways of navigating life’s ups and downs with other people having similar experiences. Most weeks focus on open support and conversation; once a month, we feature a mini-skills workshop on building coping tools, identifying and understanding emotions, and strengthening your ability to bounce back and regulate. No registration required — just drop in when you can.

To join, simply arrive to SSB 4.600 or click the Comet Calendar link a few minutes before the start time. If you’d like reminders and an easier check-in, you can also message us at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to be added to the roster.

These groups provide an opportunity for support from others who hold similar identities or life experiences. Participation is open and drop-in style, meaning members do not have to be current clients of the Student Counseling Center, and you may attend meetings as often or as seldom as you like. Support groups are open to all UTD students, and no group screening is required. Please note support groups are not the same as therapy groups in that they are more focused on building community and peer support guided by one of our therapists than in-depth therapeutic intervention.

title: Understanding Self & Others - Process Group
description_text:
Understanding Self & Others is a weekly interpersonal process group for students who want to explore personal growth and increase self-awareness to enhance their experiences in personal and academic settings. In this safe space, group members can practice communicating more honestly and effectively with others while gaining support from peers. Group topics may include adjustment, loneliness, academic/general stress, and relationships.
 

Process groups are focused on the exploration and open processing and discussion of participants. Process groups are led by one of our therapists and typically more open-ended and less structured around a specific lesson or topic for the day. Clients are required to complete a group screening to assess whether the group matches their needs and interest.

For process groups, if you are not a current or recent client, please make an appointment to get started and note your interest in group therapy. You’ll complete intake paperwork and have a 30-minute “IC” (individual consultation) with one of our therapists, and then get scheduled for a brief screening meeting with the group’s leader.

If you are a current or recent client, reach out to our Groups & Workshops Coordinator at sccgroups@utdallas.edu to schedule a screening meeting.

title: Virtual Book Launch and Discussion: Hannah Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism
description_text:
Register for our upcoming virtual book launch and discussion of the new critical edition of Hannah Arendt’s The Origins of Totalitarianism, featuring a conversation with its four editors.

Following our September book launch at The University of Texas at Dallas, the Ackerman Center for Holocaust Studies is delighted to continue the conversation online and welcome a wider audience to explore this landmark work.

First published in 1951, The Origins of Totalitarianism has remained a major point of reference and debate across generations of scholars and readers. Published in summer 2026, the new critical edition brings together the final English and German versions of Arendt’s work, alongside earlier drafts, archival materials, and detailed scholarly annotations.

Join editors Annette Vowinckel, Hanno Berger, Christian Pischel, and Elena Stingl for a virtual discussion exploring the making of this critical edition, its scholarly significance, and the new possibilities it offers for reading and interpreting Arendt’s influential work. The conversation will also reflect on the questions Arendt's work continues to raise about antisemitism, imperialism, and totalitarianism, and the relevance of her ideas to the contemporary world.

title: Physics Colloquium – Dr. Shyam Menon, Flatiron Institute
description_text:
Forming star clusters across cosmic time: from our nearby Universe to cosmic dawn

It is well established that stars rarely form alone. Instead, they are born alongside other stars in clusters and associations within galaxies. Yet most stars observed in our cosmic neighborhood do not seem to reside in gravitationally bound clusters, in stark contrast to globular clusters—stellar systems that have remained bound for over ten billion years. In this talk, I will argue that the clues to these distinct outcomes are embedded in the physics of how stars form out of dense gas in galaxies, and how newborn stars subsequently influence their immediate surroundings. Drawing on insights from radiation hydrodynamical simulations, I will demonstrate how this interplay changes in the early Universe to form objects resembling globular clusters, and emphasize their dramatic influence on their host galaxies. Finally, I will highlight how these insights may be central to several outstanding puzzles raised by James Webb Space Telescope observations of the early Universe, and discuss ongoing efforts to address critical theoretical and computational challenges in connecting these pieces.

Bio: Shyam Menon is a Flatiron Research Fellow at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Astrophysics. He received his Ph.D. in astrophysics from the Australian National University in 2023, working with Christoph Federrath and Mark Krumholz. His doctoral thesis earned the Astronomical Society of Australia’s 2024 Charlene Heisler Prize. His research combines numerical simulations and theoretical modeling to study star formation, stellar feedback, and their role in galaxy evolution.

In this group clients will gain a deeper and affirming understanding of their emotions and be empowered with knowledge and skills to use their emotions in a fulfilling way. They will also have the opportunity to find resonance and connection with those who face similar life experiences. Group is based on Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy. 

Skills-based groups are focused on building skills to help improve one’s life and tend to be based around a theme or topic (e.g., learning coping skills, distress management, improved self-compassion, etc.). This type of group is led by one of our therapists and includes a combination of both learning skills and sharing about personal experiences.

title: Dr. Chan Hyun Park
description_text:
The Role of Strategic Problem Formulation in Search: Evidence from the Field 

Recent research highlights that problem formulation, or theorizing the causes behind performance feedback, allows more effective search. Comprehensive formulations presumably compress complex problem spaces into their central dimensions, helping leaders find valuable solutions while avoiding suboptimal ones. We propose that for strategic problems, which are ill-structured, formulations are also generative. Because such problems lack complete information, leaders draw on idiosyncratic beliefs and experiences to fill the gaps. Formulations therefore identify new dimensions not prescribed by performance feedback, allowing more distant search and revealing new opportunities for value creation. This value is distinct from that of the intensive, local search that performance feedback prompts. A longitudinal field study of 179 leaders of Chinese agricultural firms and an experiment with 216 MBA students generally support our model.

title: Data Science and Statistics Seminar by Dr. Patrick Brandt (UT Dallas EPPS)
description_text:
Title: Forecasting Accurately in Space and Time (FAST): Explainability for End-Users

Abstract: Quantitative forecasts of conflict and violence should be understandable for end-users, including governments, IOs, NGOs, journalists, and private enterprise. In this paper, we report our efforts at explanation in the context of a policy transfer activity: the Fast Forward: Forecasting Global Emerging Threats Competition. Along with conflict forecasts, this competition required teams to submit machine-generated explanations for each forecast, to be assessed by intelligence analysts. An explanation interface must do several things to effectively inform analysts, but most importantly we argue that explanations should contextualize the forecast, recognize its limits, and understand its applicability for a purpose. We found value in four elements of explanations:  (1) textual bottom-line-up-front summaries; (2) graphical representations of time trends alongside forecasts; (3) graphical representations of input data, including where the geographic unit sits in the global distribution; and (4) comparisons of the forecast to the global set of forecasts. We explain the development of our underlying models and the format and processes for generating explanations and visualizing results. This serves as an initial template for others to replicate, build on, and modify for their own purposes.

Authors: Scott Robert Patterson, Patrick T. Brandt, Vito D’Orazio, Max Z. Margulies and Theodore McLauchlin

title: Powering the AI Era: Energy-Efficient Power Delivery for Next-Generation 3D Ics by Professor Deukhyoun Heo (from Washington State University)
description_text:
Bio: 

Deukhyoun Heo (Fellow, IEEE) received his Ph.D. degree in electrical and computer engineering from the Georgia Institute of Technology in 2000. He joined National Semiconductor as a Senior Design Engineer in 2000 and Washington State University in 2003, where he is currently the Frank Brands Analog Distinguished Professor of Electrical Engineering.

     He has authored approximately 200 publications, including 100 peer-reviewed journal papers and 100 international conference papers. His research focuses on energy-efficient power delivery and power management ICs for next-generation AI computing, high-efficiency hybrid DC–DC converters, intelligent power delivery networks for advanced 3D ICs, mm-wave/sub-THz transceivers, phased-array beamformers, and AI-assisted RF circuit design.

     Dr. Heo has served on IEEE MTT-S technical program committees and as Associate Editor of IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems II: Express Briefs and IEEE Transactions on Microwave Theory and Techniques. He currently serves as Associate Editor of IEEE Transactions on Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) Systems and IEEE Microwave and Wireless Technology Letters. His honors include the 2000 IEEE IMS Best Student Paper Award, NSF CAREER Award (2009), and IEEE Fellow elevation (2024).
 

 

Abstract: 

As artificial intelligence drives semiconductor integration beyond conventional 2D scaling, emerging 3D IC technologies—including through-silicon vias (TSVs), hybrid bonding, and monolithic 3D (M3D) integration—promise unprecedented computing performance and density. Yet, a critical bottleneck remains: how can we efficiently deliver massive power to increasingly dense, low-voltage AI processors?

This talk addresses this challenge through innovative high-step-down hybrid DC–DC converters that combine switched-capacitor and inductor-based architectures for efficient power delivery from high-voltage buses to sub-1-V computing loads. Reconfigurable single- and multi-output converters are introduced to reduce power losses and improve power density. Looking ahead, we envision intelligent, workload-adaptive power delivery networks that integrate converter reconfiguration, voltage–frequency islands, and learning-assisted optimization to redefine energy efficiency in next-generation AI computing systems.

Rescues Adversity-Induced Maternal Motivation Deficits.

Maternal behavior relies on mesolimbic dopamine signaling to assign reinforcing value to infant cues and drive motivated caregiving behaviors, but environmental adversity can disrupt these processes. title: Neuroscience First Year Presentation: Ivelize Freire
description_text:
Please join us

Tuesday, December 1, 2026

4:00pm – 4:30pm CST

NSERL 3.204

for a First Year Presentation by

 

Ivelize Freire 

University of Texas at Dallas

Investigating Vagus nerve stimulation as a neuro-immune 

therapy for enhancing nerve regeneration 

 

Peripheral nerve injury (PNI) refers to damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, disrupting axonal communication and triggering a series of degenerative and regenerative processes, including Wallerian degeneration (WD). Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) can activate the inflammatory reflex, potentially modulating the inflammatory response following PNI. We hypothesized that initiating VNS three days post-injury, during a period of substantial macrophage infiltration, would modulate neuroinflammation, promote nerve regeneration, and improve sensorimotor outcomes. Our findings suggest that early VNS may alter the neuroinflammatory environment following PNI, as evidenced by significant differences in CD163+ macrophage abundance across nerve regions. These changes may be associated with altered sensory recovery but not motor recovery.

title: Lecture by Nan Z. Da: "The Forest of Inference"
description_text:
Abstract: Shakespeare's Tragedy of King Lear has been important to literary criticism, especially the contingent that worries about being wronged and about wronging others. It is in the discussion of Lear that the terms “data” and “critical data” show up in literary studies for the first time: “data” in an 1819 lecture by Samuel Coleridge and “critical data” in an influential 1987 essay by Stanley Cavell. Both critics saw in Lear an agonized relationship to the scientific method and other tenets of empiricism. Among other empirical difficulties, Lear successfully triggers the responses — such as over-identification, projection, transference, and punitiveness— that cause readers and playgoers to gravely misremember the plot and even stick with those mistakes. Lear is about this kind of vulnerability and has been probed for this vulnerability at least since Coleridge. No other work of literature has placed as much stress on interpretive validity. This talk will expand on the spot to which Lear pins literary criticism, the spot where data becomes inference, first described as significant and troublesome in Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding. 

Bio: Nan Z. Da is Associate Professor of English at The Johns Hopkins University. She has published extensively on a wide variety of subjects, ranging from nineteenth-century American literature to transatlantic philosophy--and from the history of Maoist trauma to the intersection of literary studies and the data sciences. She is the author of Intransitive Encounter: Sino-U.S. Literatures and the Limits of Exchange (Columbia University Press, 2018) and The Chinese Tragedy of King Lear (Princeton University Press, 2025). Her essays have appeared in journals such as New Left Review, PMLA, New Literary History, American Literary History, and Critical Inquiry. Professor Da is currently at work on two books: "Disambiguation, a Tragedy: Criticism and Writing from the Chinese Diaspora" and "Literary Studies, Data Science, and the Future of Prejudice." 

Professor Da's lecture is co-sponsored by Language & Literature and the Center for Asian Studies.

title: Modeling, Predicting, and Designing 3D Genome Organization
description_text:
Featured Speaker Dr. Bin Zhang from Boston University presenting from 3-4pm in NSERL 3rd floor room RL 3.204

Abstract:

The genome’s three-dimensional folding is encoded in its sequence and shapes how genes are regulated, but turning that relationship into a quantitative, usable framework requires understanding the physical principles of folding, predicting structures where experiments are unavailable, and ultimately reversing the map to engineer function. Here I will describe a path through these three steps.

We first use maximum entropy optimization to build nucleosome-resolution chromatin models consistent with experimental data. These models show that euchromatin forms condensed domains with short active regions on their surface, a picture that reconciles the compaction of euchromatin with its accessibility for transcription. Because experimental contact data are not always available, we next developed ChromoGen, a diffusion model that predicts ensembles of single-cell chromatin conformations from sequence-derived information. Our latest generalization extends ChromoGen to 20 Mb regions at 5 kb resolution, capturing structural heterogeneity without requiring any contact data.  Finally, we introduce CRAFT, a multimodal DNA language model that jointly predicts gene expression and Hi-C contacts and can be used to design sequences. By linking sequence, structure and function in one model, CRAFT moves from describing genome organization to programming it.

title: Workshop Talk with Charissa Terranova, “Biological Bill of Rights: Moholy’s Space-Time Social Democracy”
description_text:
Artist and designer Laszlo Moholy-Nagy described his last book Vision in Motion (1947) as an attempt to add a "biological bill of rights" to the "politico-social." This talk explores the meaning of this elliptical but enchanting phrase in the context of Moholy-Nagy's final posthumously published work and the development of the American welfare state in the postwar period.

Charissa N. Terranova is a writer and educator researching nature, biology, and biotechnology in the history of art and architecture. She is a Margaret M. McDermott Distinguished Chair in Art and Aesthetic Studies and Professor of Art and Architectural History in the Bass School of Arts, Humanities, and Technology at the Univeristy of Texas at Dallas. Terranova has authored several books and articles about the interstices of history in the plural, that is histories of art, design, science, and technology.

This event is in-person only. RSVP: Heather.Bowling@utdallas.edu

title: Dissertation Proposal Defense - Maedeh Vahid
description_text:
Please join us

Tuesday, December 8, 2026

4:00pm – 5:00pm CST

NSERL 3.204

for a Dissertation Proposal Defense 

by 

Maedeh Vahid

 

 

 

  The role of prelimbic cortex neuronal ensembles in alcohol relapse and cognitive flexibility

Alcohol use disorder is a chronic, relapsing condition characterized by compulsive alcohol seeking despite adverse consequences. Impaired cognitive flexibility is among the cognitive deficits associated with chronic alcohol exposure and may contribute to relapse vulnerability. The prelimbic cortex (PL), a subregion of the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), plays an important role in regulating both drug-seeking behavior and cognitive flexibility. However, the neuronal populations and circuits underlying these behaviors remain poorly understood. Our preliminary findings show that prolonged alcohol exposure impairs cognitive flexibility, while chemogenetic inhibition of the mPFC reduces cue-induced alcohol seeking and improves cognitive flexibility. These findings suggest that mPFC activity contributes to both behaviors, but whether they involve overlapping neuronal ensembles within the PL or depend on distinct downstream projection pathways remains unknown. This proposal aims to determine whether alcohol seeking and cognitive flexibility recruit shared PL neuronal ensembles and investigate their projections to the nucleus accumbens core and mediodorsal thalamus. Using activity-dependent neuronal tagging, projection-specific approaches, and in vivo calcium imaging, we will examine the functional contributions of these ensembles and how their activity is altered by alcohol exposure.

Into the Abyss: Rabbi Aron Tänzer on German History, Antisemitism, and Liberal Democracy
description_text:
Register for a virtual talk, "Into the Abyss: Rabbi Aron Tänzer on German History, Antisemitism, and Liberal Democracy," featuring Dr. Christopher J. Probst on Wednesday, December 9, 2026, at 12:00 p.m. CT. 

About the Talk

This talk will provide a perspective that offers an especially unique contribution to our understanding of German history from 1929–1949. Dr. Probst considers the life and work of Rabbi Aron Tänzer of Göppingen, whose Jewish community was decimated during the Holocaust. His is the extraordinary story of a man who comforted his congregation, carefully documented Jewish history, and fought antisemitism as the Nazis came to power. Yet the small Jewish community that he cared for no longer exists. His life and work give us a glimpse of German history in the waning years of the Weimar Republic and the rise of Hitler and the Nazis through Jewish eyes. 

About the Speaker

Christopher J. Probst is a historian, educator, and museum education consultant with a Ph.D. in History from Royal Holloway, University of London. His book, Demonizing the Jews: Luther and the Protestant Church in Nazi Germany, was published in 2012. He has since published many essays and articles about Protestant-Jewish relations in Germany before, during, and after the Holocaust. In 2008, Chris was a Charles H. Revson Foundation Fellow at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. In 2025, he created a Substack publication, Echoes from the Past, which offers weekly perspectives - some contemporary and reflective, others a bit more academic - on history, religion, antisemitism, and intolerance, with a focus on the Holocaust.

for a First Year Presentation by

 

Melissa Salazar

Early Life Programming of Affective and Nociceptive Behaviors and

Immune Profile Across the Lifespan

 

This research examines how early life adversity resulting from resource scarcity influences behavioral, pain-related, and neuroimmune outcomes across development. Using a rodent model of early life scarcity-adversity, affective and nociceptive responses were assessed during adolescence, adulthood, and aging, alongside characterization of microglial morphology in the adult amygdala. Findings revealed sex differences in exploratory behavior, reward-related behavior, and thermal sensitivity during adolescence and adulthood, while preliminary findings suggest early life adversity may shift adult amygdala microglia toward an activated state. Together, these findings provide insight into how early environmental conditions may alter lifelong behavioral and immune function within the amygdala and may contribute to health disparities associated with socioeconomic status.

Natalia Valderrama

Silphion-derived compounds exhibit analgesic properties in vitro 

Pain management relies on our knowledge of underlying mechanisms driving nociceptive neuron sensitization. To address the need for next generation non-addictive analgesics, we sought to use natural products that have binding affinity to Sigma 2 Receptor (S2R). In this present study, a natural putative-S2R ligand with 2,000 years of history known as Silphion, was evaluated in vitro for potential modulatory effects on the Integrated Stress Response (ISR) and spontaneous electrical firing in human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) nociceptors. Using immunocytochemistry (ICC) and multielectrode array assay (MEA), silphion-derived compounds significantly reduced ISR levels in cultured primary mouse dorsal root ganglia (DRG) and silenced hiPSC nociceptors through sodium channel-dependent excitability. These preliminary results provide insight into a potential template for future pain therapies.

Bios:

Music by Robert Xavier Rodríguez has been performed by conductors such as Sir Neville Marriner, Antal Dorati, Eduardo Mata, James DePriest, Sir Raymond Leppard, Keith Lockhart, Andrew Litton and Leonard Slatkin and by such organizations as the New York City Opera, Brooklyn Academy of Music, Vienna Schauspielhaus, Dallas Opera, Houston Grand Opera, Vienna Schauspielhaus, Israel Philharmonic, Mexico City Philharmonic, Cleveland Orchestra and the Seattle, Houston, Dallas, Pittsburgh, Indianapolis, Baltimore, St. Louis, National, Boston and Chicago Symphonies.  He has received a Guggenheim Fellowship, the Goddard Lieberson Award from the American Academy of Arts and Letters, the Prix Lili Boulanger and the Prix de Composition Prince Pierre de Monaco.  Rodríguez has served as Composer-in-Residence with the San Antonio Symphony and the Dallas Symphony.  Twenty CDs featuring his music have been recorded (1999 Grammy nomination), and his music is published exclusively by G. Schirmer.  He is Professor of Music at the University of Texas at Dallas, where he holds an Endowed Chair of Art and Aesthetic Studies and is Director of the Musica Nova Ensemble.

Pianist Mikhail Berestnev studied at the Russian Academy of Music, TCU (Artist Diploma) and SMU (Performance Diploma).  He has won prizes at the Delphic Games and the Stanislav Neuhaus Competitions in Russia, the Sydney International Competition, the BNDES International Piano Competition in Rio de Janeiro, and the Maria Canals International Piano Competition in Barcelona.  He was also a semifinalist in the Queen Elisabeth International Piano Competition in Brussels.  He has performed with many Russian orchestras as well as the TCU, Sydney, San Angelo and Brazilian Symphonies, the Royal Chamber Orchestra of Wallonia and the Fort Worth Symphony Orchestra.  He is also active in chamber music, including performances with musicians from leading Russian Orchestras such as the Symphony Orchestra of the Bolshoi Theatre and the ensembles Moscow Virtuosi and Musica Viva.
